doc.title: Nicki Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe. Utica, New York, November 6, 2010 [interview 1 of 2]

title: How a bassist reads a gig: groove, Dick Hyman, Jeff Hamilton
summary: She describes finding what each gig requires, keeping the groove steady, and following drummers like Jeff Hamilton; Dick Hyman gives guidelines without instructions.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Um. Well it’s funny, there are different ways to lead a band, you know, and now that I’m a band leader myself a lot I’m learning how to do it and get the results and get the respect and everything, and there are some people, like when I was up here last time I worked with Dick Hyman here, and I also worked with Dick Hyman earlier in the year at Merlin’s. And someone like Dick doesn’t really want to tell you how to play but might give you a guideline, you know what I mean? Like well I think you sing that song better, or just come in after a couple of choruses. And that’s like you get a little bit of a guideline but he’ll never tell you actually how to play the gig. And so I think you’ve got to use your best judgement. But you have to learn ahead of the gig. I always tell students that. You have to, unless you’re leading you don’t play bass solos behind the clarinet solo. You know? You don’t do that. You play what the gig requires, which, for me, is a groove, it’s time, it’s a feel, it’s a sound. And I love accompanying. So I’m always finding out — if the drum is getting really busy I might play simple. If it’s getting exciting well I might rhythmically push too. You know what I mean? So you have to kind of just keep your wits about you. But I think what the thing about being a bass player is you really like the groove. So if it’s all going crazy around you you’ve got to be like the center and be like I’m not going to let this slow down or go out the window, you’ve really got to keep your center and just try to make all of that work somehow. Sometimes it does, sometimes not so well.

That’s great advice. I’ve often felt that the bass player really is the lynchpin of the whole thing. I mean you can send the music in a direction if you want to, I mean if you want to start swinging and the rest of the band is playing in two, you can sort of like say no, we’re going this way.
And you have a lot of power it seems to me.

It is, and sometimes you play with — if I’m at a gig say, and I remember being on the gig once with Jeff Hamilton out in California, a wonderful drummer. Now when I was playing with Jeff, and we hadn’t played together before, I’m going to let Jeff lead, even though he may not be leading the set, you know what I mean, but we’re in a trio or a quartet and someone’s out front playing, I forget who it was at the time. But my eyes were on Jeff. Whatever Jeff does I’m going to — so I noticed when he was in two, and I just tried to follow his lead. Some drummers are really good at leading and you can just follow along. And other times you feel like you know what I mean, you can take more of it. It’s really a communication. I like the communication between bass players and drummers. It makes the music that much more tighter.
Is there such a thing as playing, you hear the term, playing on top of the beat or behind the beat?
